summary: Provides a framework for developing protocol extensions so GMPLS and PCE can control Optical Transport Networks as specified in ITU-T G.709 (2012 edition). It is a framework document, with the detailed protocol work left to other documents.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7062 is about the part of the internet that moves data as light. Optical transport networks carry client signals inside containers of different sizes, and the newer ITU-T standard added new containers and a finer slot size. The RFC explains what changed and what the network's control software would have to be able to do to build those new connections automatically, rather than by hand.

subtitle: How the routing and signalling protocols of a GMPLS control plane should be extended to steer optical transport networks.

tldr.problem: The signalling extensions for optical transport networks were written against the 2001 edition of the ITU-T G.709 standard, so the newer containers, slot sizes and flexible-rate signals that operators now deploy cannot be controlled by a GMPLS control plane.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reviews what changed in G.709, then lists what the signalling, routing and link management protocols need in order to set up and route those new signals, and how a network with old and new equipment side by side can be controlled.
tldr.outcome: The document is a framework, not a protocol. It fixes the scope to the ODU layer, leaves the wavelength layer to another document, and hands the actual extension work to later specifications.

today: RFC 7062 is an Informational RFC published in November 2013, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a framework that sets out requirements; the protocol extensions themselves are left to other documents, and control of the wavelength layer is left to RFC 6163.

sections.title: Why Optical Networks Need a Control Plane
sections.content:
Optical Transport Networks have become a mainstream layer 1 technology for the transport network. Operators want to add control-plane capabilities based on GMPLS to optical transport networks, to gain the benefits of a high-function control plane such as improved network resiliency and better use of resources.

GMPLS extends Multi-Protocol Label Switching to cover time division multiplexing networks, such as SONET and SDH, PDH and G.709 sub-lambda, lambda switching optical networks, and spatial switching, where an incoming port or fibre is mapped to an outgoing port or fibre. The architecture is in RFC 3945, the signalling function and RSVP-TE extensions in RFC 3471 and RFC 3473, the routing and OSPF extensions in RFC 4202 and RFC 4203, and the Link Management Protocol in RFC 4204.

The signalling extensions in RFC 4328 give basic GMPLS control of optical transport networks as described in the 2001 revision of the G.709 specification. The 2012 revision adds new features, including various multiplexing structures, two types of tributary slot at 1.25 Gbps and 2.5 Gbps, and an extension of the ODUj definition to include the ODUflex function. This document reviews the parts of that change that affect the control-plane protocols, explains why and how to update the mechanisms in RFC 4328, provides a framework for GMPLS control of optical transport networks, and discusses the implications for a Path Computation Element.
sections.plainLanguage: Fibre networks were once built by hand, with an engineer deciding every connection. A control plane is the software that decides those connections automatically. This RFC is about making that software able to handle the newer kinds of optical container that operators now use.

sections.title: The Containers
sections.content:
For the purposes of the control plane, the optical transport network is treated as made of ODU and wavelength layers. This document focuses on the ODU layer, and control of the wavelength layer is out of scope and covered elsewhere.

Client signals are mapped into a lower order ODU container, and those containers are multiplexed onto the higher order container that rides on a wavelength. A LO ODU is the container carrying a client of the optical transport network, either mapped directly into an OTUk where the indices match, or multiplexed into a larger server container. A HO ODU transports a multiplex of lower order signals in its payload area. An ODUflex is the flexible container: it can have any bit rate, with a bit rate tolerance of +/-100 ppm. Throughout the document, ODUj refers to containers acting as lower order ODUs and ODUk to containers used as higher order ODUs.

The remaining terms are the surrounding structure: OPU is the Optical Channel Payload Unit, OTU the Optical Channel Transport Unit, OMS the Optical Multiplex Section, MSI the Multiplex Structure Identifier, and TPN the Tributary Port Number. The signal hierarchy is client signal, then ODUj, then OTU and OCh together, then OMS, with the individual OTU and OCh signals combined in the OMS by wavelength division multiplexing to form the link between the nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of the optical network as a set of boxes. A client signal goes into a small box, small boxes are packed into a bigger box, and the bigger boxes ride on light. The RFC fixes the vocabulary for naming these boxes.

sections.title: Mapping, Multiplexing and Slots
sections.content:
The 2012 G.709 revision defines the lower order containers ODU0, ODU1, ODU2, ODU2e, ODU3, ODU4 and ODUflex, with their nominal bit rates. The fixed containers have a tolerance of +/-20 ppm, while ODU2e and both forms of ODUflex have a tolerance of +/-100 ppm. Circuit clients are proportionally wrapped, so the bit rate follows the client signal and the tolerance is fixed. Packet clients are mapped using the Generic Framing Procedure, and the recommendation is that an ODUflex fill an integral number of tributary slots of the smallest higher order container over which it may be carried.

Links between switching nodes are provided by one or more wavelengths. Each wavelength carries one optical channel, which carries one OTU, which carries one ODU. The lower order containers are mapped into the tributary slots of the higher order payload. The initial versions of G.709 referenced by RFC 4328 provided a single slot granularity of 2.5 Gbps; the 2012 revision added a granularity of 1.25 Gbps. OTU1 offers one slot at 2.5 Gbps or two at 1.25 Gbps, OTU2 offers four or eight, OTU3 sixteen or thirty-two, and OTU4 only the finer granularity with eighty slots. Because the actual slot bit rate depends on the container, the number of slots a given container occupies varies: an ODU2e uses nine slots in an OTU3 but only eight in an OTU4.

Multiplexing one container into a larger one also needs in-band information so that the far end can demultiplex correctly. This is the MSI information, carried in the payload overhead and local to each link. It has one entry per slot, each holding a payload type and a tributary port number, which is the same for all the slots carrying one instance of the same container. On every node and link two values must be provisioned: the transmitted MSI inserted by the source of the trail, and the expected MSI used to check the accepted MSI received in band after a three-frame integration. If the two do not match, the traffic is dropped and a payload mismatch alarm is raised.
sections.plainLanguage: Slots are the fixed-width compartments inside a bigger container, and the new standard offers two widths of them. When several small containers are packed together, each slot also carries a note saying what is in it and which port it belongs to, and the far end checks that note against what it expected.

sections.title: How Connections Are Made
sections.content:
Connection management in optical transport networks is about controlling the connectivity of ODU paths and of optical channels; this document is concerned with the ODU paths. Recent ITU-T architecture work models the ODU as a single-layer network with the bit rate as a parameter of links and connections, rather than as a set of layers as SDH was. Links and nodes can then be seen in a single topology as a common set of resources, available to provide ODUj connections whatever the value of j. The OTU and OCh layers should be visible in a single topological representation of the network, and from a logical point of view they may be treated as the same switchable entity.

Two topologies matter to the control plane. In the first, the ODU links are presented between adjacent nodes, which are Optical Digital Cross Connects, and there are links with a variety of slots available. A request for an ODUj connection between two nodes needs a path that has the required number of free slots and offers the lowest cost, and signalling then sets up that path and tells each transit node which slots to use so that it can map, multiplex and demultiplex as required.

In the second, the nodes interconnect with wavelength switched nodes capable of optical channel switching, so there is an ODU layer and an OCh layer and the network is a multi-layer network. The operator chooses whether the real optical channel topology is visible to the ODU path computation or hidden behind a cloud. In the visible case, a request for a lower order connection is answered by asking the optical channel domain for a higher order or optical channel connection between the two nodes, and that connection appears at the ODU level as a forwarding adjacency used to build the requested connection.
sections.plainLanguage: To build a connection, the control software has to find a route with enough free space in it and then tell every node along the route which slots to use. The operator also decides whether the software sees the wavelength layer underneath or treats it as a black box.

sections.title: What the Control Protocols Have to Learn
sections.content:
Path computation for an optical connection is done in two layers, optical channel and OTUk on one side and ODUj on the other, and the hierarchy of label switched paths that connects them is defined in RFC 4206 and RFC 6107. The same hierarchy can be used inside the ODU layers, so that one ODUj connection is nested inside another ODUk connection. That is how a network with newer services can be introduced without upgrading every element: a few dedicated boards tunnel the new services through the legacy containers, and the outer connection is advertised as a forwarding adjacency.

The signalling protocol needs several extensions. It must be able to name the new signal types and carry the traffic parameters for them, and for ODUflex the bit rate has to be carried as well because the other types have fixed rates that can be deduced from the type. It must identify the slot granularity used when setting up a path. A new label format is needed to carry the exact slot allocation information for the extended mapping and multiplexing, for example an ODU0 into ODU2 multiplexing at 1.25 Gbps granularity. There must be a mechanism for allocating and negotiating the tributary port numbers used in the MSI information, support for virtual concatenation of an ODUk signal with k equal to 1, 2 or 3 and for the link capacity adjustment scheme, and support for the hitless adjustment of ODUflex, which needs every node along the path to take part and so is better driven by signalling than by hand.

The routing protocol needs to carry enough information to compute a route. It must convey which lower order container types a link can multiplex, and enough bandwidth information to reserve the right number of slots for any fixed container or for ODUflex. It must distinguish a link that can terminate signals from one that can only switch them. It must advertise the slot granularity, because the two ends of a path must match. It must support up to eight priority levels for resource reservation and the bundling of several OTU links between the same pair of nodes. The link management protocol must correlate the two ends of a link, both on slot granularity and on which lower order container types and multiplexing hierarchies each end supports, since one end might support ODU0 into ODU1 into ODU3 while the other supports ODU0 into ODU2 into ODU3.

Backward compatibility only needs thought for ODU1, ODU2 and ODU3 connections, because the legacy optical transport network supports only those three signal types. A node that supports only the new procedures leaves the two kinds of node unable to jointly control a path. A node that supports both can decide which set of procedures to follow from the switching capability advertised in routing, from the switching type received in signalling, or from the switching capability advertised by the next hop. Path computation elements must carry the new signal types and variable bandwidth information in their requests, and management must be able to handle both the legacy network and the new features, through either a network management system or the control plane.
sections.plainLanguage: The list is long but each item is simple: the signalling has to be able to name the new container types and say how wide the slots are, the routing has to know how much room each link really has, and the two ends of every link have to agree on the slot size before a connection can cross it.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
Using control-plane protocols for signalling, routing and path computation opens an optical transport network to security threats through attacks on those protocols. The RFC's judgement is that this is not greater than the risk presented by the existing optical transport control plane. The data communication network for the optical GMPLS control-plane protocols is likely to be in the in-fibre overhead, which, together with access lists at the network edges, provides a significant security feature.

For the detail of specific security measures, the RFC points to the documents that define the protocols: RFC 3473, RFC 4203, RFC 5307, RFC 4204 and RFC 5440. RFC 5920 gives an overview of security vulnerabilities and protection mechanisms for the GMPLS control plane.
sections.plainLanguage: Adding a control plane does not add much new risk: the control messages travel inside the fibre's own overhead and the network edge filters who may talk to it. The RFC points to the protocol documents for the details.

layers.detail: The customer's traffic entering the network

layers.detail: The container the client signal is mapped into

layers.detail: Optical multiplex section: wavelengths combined into the link

viz.caption: WHERE THE CONTROL PROTOCOLS NEED EXTENDING

items.title: Signalling
items.text: Name the new signal types, carry the ODUflex bit rate, and set the slot granularity.

items.title: Slot allocation
items.text: A new label format for the exact slots chosen on each link.

items.title: Routing
items.text: Carry the link's multiplexing capability, real slot bandwidth and slot granularity.

items.title: Link management
items.text: Make the two ends of a link agree on granularity and on supported containers.

items.title: Backward compatibility
items.text: Decide, per node and per path, whether to use the old or the new procedures.

items.title: Path computation
items.text: Carry the new signal types and variable bandwidth into path requests.
